sections.title: 📋 Cart Operations & Visitor Engagement
sections.text: cart-operations-visitor-engagement 📋 Cart Operations & Visitor Engagement Marine Mammal Cart Operating instructions and visitor guidance from May 20, 2026 Field Observations. Visitor interactions: Guests may touch the marine mammal models, but should not lift or carry them. Mentioning model weights is optional. Activating videos: Position the black puck over the corresponding activation area. If no video starts, move the puck slightly until the animal profile border turns yellow. If a video still does not work: Contact an available specialist for assistance. Continue engaging visitors using the specimens and interpretive talking points. Training materials: Consult the Marine Mammal Cart training handout and Naturalist Library marine mammal pages for additional background. Unresolved operating questions: Ask the current shift captain or available specialist; do not assume the location of keys or other procedures that have not been confirmed. Invite visitors to examine the specimens without lifting them. Ask visitors what they notice about the structures and how each mammal uses them. If a video fails, use the physical specimens to keep the conversation going. cart operations visitor engagement May 20 2026 training video puck

sections.title: 🐋 Blue Whale Ear Bone
sections.text: blue-whale-ear-bone 🐋 Blue Whale Ear Bone Marine Mammal Cart Blue whale hearing, songs, migration, krill feeding, and Monterey Bay connections. Male blue whales are the loudest animals on the planet! Their calls to find females can be heard up to 1,000 miles away. Their survival literally depends on their ability to hear one another. However, the ocean is becoming an increasingly noisy place, mostly due to shipping noise. Luckily, our bay and the surrounding waters are part of a sanctuary, so commercial vessels give the area a wide berth to reduce underwater noise pollution. Simple steps like this will help blue whale populations continue to grow. Currently, the North Eastern Pacific population is around 2,000 blue whales. The blue whales that visit Monterey Bay spend their winters in warm tropical waters near Costa Rica where pregnant mothers give birth to their calves. But, there's not much to eat there. Each spring, they migrate thousands of miles to feast in the nutrient-rich waters of Monterey Bay, where krill, a tiny shrimp-like animal, occurs in huge swarms during most springs and summers. A single blue whale can eat more than 5,000 pounds of krill every day. Specimen label: Blue whale ear bone English: Blue whales can hear one another's calls a thousand miles apart. Spanish: Las ballenas azules pueden oír los llamados de otras a mil millas de distancia. Discussion prompt: Why do male blue whales sing? English: Male blue whales sing songs to find females over vast distances. Spanish: Las ballenas azules macho cantan para encontrar hembras a gran distancia. Discussion prompt: Why do blue whales visit Monterey Bay? English: Blue whales migrate thousands of miles to strain krill from the bay. Spanish: Las ballenas azules migran recorriendo miles de millas para filtrar krill de la bahía. mmc blue whale ear bone hearing migration krill monterey bay marine mammal

sections.title: 🐬 Dolphin Jaw
sections.text: dolphin-jaw 🐬 Dolphin Jaw Marine Mammal Cart Dolphin hearing, echolocation, teamwork, prey herding, and Monterey Bay visits. Dolphins like these have a great trick up their sleeve to help find and catch prey. They send out a series of high-pitched clicks, which bounce off their prey and back to their jaw, not their ear. This sound-based locating strategy means they can find food in water that has poor visibility, or even in the dark! Pacific white-sided dolphins that visit Monterey Bay don't stay year-round. They roam the west coast of the United States in search of fish and squid. When the pod discovers a school of prey, they work together cooperatively to herd the school into a tight ball, making the fish easier to catch. Specimen label: Dolphin jaw English: Dolphins hear with help from their jawbones. Spanish: Los delfines oyen con la ayuda de sus mandíbulas. Discussion prompt: How do dolphins find food in dark waters? English: Dolphins track prey by emitting clicks that bounce sound waves off prey. Spanish: Los delfines localizan a su presa emitiendo "clics" que hacen rebotar ondas sonoras contra sus presas. Discussion prompt: How does teamwork help dolphins catch prey? English: Dolphins hunt together in large pods by herding fish into a tight ball. Spanish: Los delfines cazan en grandes manadas para "arrear" peces y crear con ellos una bola compacta. mmc dolphin jaw echolocation teamwork prey marine mammal

sections.title: 🐳 Orca Tooth
sections.text: orca-tooth 🐳 Orca Tooth Marine Mammal Cart Orca teeth, salmon, gray whale migration, top predator behavior, and Monterey Bay prey. Some orcas live year-round in the waters of the Pacific Northwest. They specialize in eating fish, especially salmon. They travel south when food is scarce in their home waters, and visit our bay in search of food. Once they've found a school of salmon, orcas use clicks and whistles to communicate and coordinate with other members of the pod. Their remarkable combination of size, speed, and exceptional senses are some of the reasons why orcas are the top of the ocean food web. Each year, gray whale families pass through Monterey during long migrations between Alaska and Mexico. Some orcas specialize in eating marine mammals, including gray whales. During the peak of the gray whale's northward migration through our bay, orcas visit in search of younger, more vulnerable grays. But because Monterey Bay sees lots of marine mammals, orcas may visit year-round in search of prey. Specimen label: Orca tooth English: Orcas use their teeth to grasp and tear prey. Spanish: Las orcas usan sus dientes para sujetar y despedazar a su presa. Discussion prompt: Why do Pacific Northwest orcas visit Monterey Bay? English: When salmon are scarce in home waters, hungry orcas head south. Spanish: Cuando el salmón escasea en las aguas donde viven, las orcas hambrientas viajan hacia el sur. Discussion prompt: What species of whale is hunted by orcas in our bay? English: Gray whales migrate through our bay twice a year, attracting hungry orcas. Spanish: Dos veces por año, las ballenas grises al migrar pasan por nuestra bahía, y esto atrae a orcas hambrientas. mmc orca tooth salmon gray whale migration predator marine mammal

sections.title: 🦭 Elephant Seal Flipper
sections.text: elephant-seal-flipper 🦭 Elephant Seal Flipper Marine Mammal Cart Elephant seal flippers, recovery from near extinction, bull males, harems, and California colonies. The elephant seal's recovery from near extinction is a testament to the effectiveness of protection. Elephant seals were once hunted nearly to extinction; their blubber was used for making lamp oil. 100 years ago, there were less than 100 seals remaining. Today, large colonies of elephant seals can be found just to the north and south of Monterey Bay. Over 200,000 elephant seals call California home. Scientists consider the population healthy and robust. Large bulls, weighing up to 5,000 pounds, protect their harem of females from rival males. A successful bull can have a harem of up to 100 females! Smaller males have no chance of finding a mate, so they steer clear of beaches where larger males are already established. They can sometimes be found on local beaches, hoping that a stray female will find his territory attractive. Specimen label: Elephant seal front flipper English: An elephant seal's front flippers have five digits, like a human hand. Spanish: Las focas elefante tienen cinco dígitos en sus aletas delanteras, similares a los de una mano humana. Discussion prompt: How many northern elephant seals live in California? English: Once hunted nearly to extinction, California's elephant seals now number more than 160,000. Spanish: Alguna vez cazadas casi hasta su extinción, hoy en día el número de focas elefante supera los 160,000. Discussion prompt: Why is bigger better for male elephant seals? English: Massive bull males rule large harems, while smaller males lead bachelors' lives. Spanish: Los machos dominantes de gran tamaño controlan grandes harenes, mientras que los machos más pequeños llevan vida de solteros. mmc elephant seal flipper conservation recovery harem marine mammal

sections.title: 🦦 Sea Otter Skull
sections.text: sea-otter-skull 🦦 Sea Otter Skull Marine Mammal Cart Sea otter skull, jaws, kelp forests, urchins, tools, armpit pockets, and predator role. Otters are a top predator of urchins in our kelp forests. Urchins are herbivores who eat kelp. If they become too abundant, they can literally make a kelp forest disappear, leaving what's known as an 'urchin barren' in their wake. That's where otters come in — they eat the urchins that eat the kelp! When otters, urchins, and kelp are in balance, we have healthy kelp forests that support an entire community of algae and animals. Otters often place a rock on their chest to help open hard-shelled prey — they bang the prey against the hard surface to crack it open and get to the tasty meat inside. They might keep their favorite rock stashed in an armpit pocket! Otters also use tools while underwater; brute strength is not enough to pry an abalone loose, so the otter uses a stone as a chisel. Otters are one of the few mammals that use tools on a daily basis. But not all food requires a tool: southern sea otters eat invertebrates, not fish, so many of their prey items are soft and squishy! Specimen label: Sea otter skull English: Strong jaws and teeth help make sea otters top predators. Spanish: Poderosas mandíbulas y dientes permiten que las nutrias marinas sean consideradas un animal superdepredador. Discussion prompt: How do sea otters help kelp forests? English: Sea otters keep sea urchin populations in check so kelp forests can thrive. Spanish: Las nutrias marinas mantienen bajo control a las poblaciones de erizos de mar para que los bosques de cachiyuyo puedan prosperar. Discussion prompt: What does a sea otter hide in its pockets? English: Sea otters stash rocks in folds of fur under their arms so they can crack open food. Spanish: Las nutrias marinas guardan piedras en los pliegues de pelaje bajo sus brazos para poder partir y abrir su alimento. mmc sea otter skull kelp forest urchins tools pockets marine mammal

sections.title: 🐋 Humpback Whale Food
sections.text: humpback-whale-food 🐋 Humpback Whale Food Marine Mammal Cart Humpback whale food, Monterey Bay feeding, migration, schooling fish, and bubble-net feeding. Humpbacks visit our bay each spring and summer for the same reason that people have fished here for thousands of years. These humpbacks spend their winters in the warm waters of Costa Rica, but travel thousands of miles to feast in Monterey Bay. Even mothers with newborn calves make the journey! But the trip is worth it — our rich waters provide an all-you-can-eat buffet. Humpbacks in Alaska work as a team when hunting for schooling fish. Once underwater, several of the humpbacks encircle the fish with a 'bubble net', which the fish won't cross. Other whales position themselves below the school and swim upward to force the fish toward the surface. The whole group of humpbacks will lunge up through the concentrated school of fish, feasting on thousands of fish in a single mouthful. Specimen label: Humpback whale food English: Both humans and humpbacks enjoy Monterey Bay's bountiful feast. Spanish: Tanto los humanos como los rorcuales jorobados disfrutan de los abundantes manjares de la Bahía de Monterey. Discussion prompt: Why do humpbacks travel to Monterey Bay? English: Humpbacks migrate thousands of miles to feed on small schooling fishes in the bay. Spanish: Los rorcuales jorobados migran miles de millas para alimentarse de los cardúmenes de peces que hay en la bahía. Discussion prompt: Why do humpbacks blow bubbles under water? English: Humpbacks work as a team by encircling fish in a bubble net and lunging from below. Spanish: Los rorcuales funcionan como equipo. Rodean a los peces en una red de burbujas y los embisten desde abajo. mmc humpback whale food migration bubble net schooling fish monterey bay marine mammal
